claim: During movement, hippocampal place cells fire action potentials with timing that precesses relative to the hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: The discovery that during movement hippocampal place cells fire action potentials with timing that precesses relative to the hippocampal theta rhythm (O'Keefe and Recce, 1993)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to O'Keefe and Recce, 1993.

claim: Time-compressed representations of behavioral sequences occur as spike sequences within each theta cycle.
source: time-compressed representations of behavioral sequences occur as spike sequences within each theta cycle (Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Skaggs et al., 1996; Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006; Foster and Wilson, 2007.

claim: Spike sequences within theta cycles may form a neuronal substrate for episodic and spatial memory.
source: Thus, spike sequences within theta cycles may form a neuronal substrate for episodic and spatial memory (Pastalkova et al., 2008; Lisman and Redish, 2009; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pastalkova et al., 2008; Lisman and Redish, 2009; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Wikenheiser and Redish, 2015.

claim: The rate at which action potentials precess relative to the theta rhythm depends on an animal's speed of movement.
source: First, the rate at which action potentials precess relative to the theta rhythm depends on an animal's speed of movement (Geisler et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Geisler et al., 2007.

claim: Phase precession occurs along arbitrary two-dimensional trajectories.
source: Second, phase precession occurs along arbitrary two-dimensional trajectories (Huxter et al., 2008; Climer et al., 2013; Jeewajee et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huxter et al., 2008; Climer et al., 2013; Jeewajee et al., 2014.

claim: Theta sequences emerge within theta waves that propagate along the dorsoventral axis of the hippocampus.
source: Third, theta sequences emerge within theta waves that propagate along the dorsoventral axis of the hippocampus (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Patel et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lubenov and Siapas, 2009; Patel et al., 2012.

claim: Place cells across the dorsoventral axis have field sizes that vary over an order of magnitude.
source: Fourth, while place cells across the dorsoventral axis have field sizes that vary over an order of magnitude, spike phase nevertheless usually advances by a maximum of a single theta cycle across their place field indicating that the rate of phase precession varies dorsoventrally (Kjelstrup et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kjelstrup et al., 2008.

claim: Spike phase usually advances by a maximum of a single theta cycle across place fields, indicating that the rate of phase precession varies dorsoventrally.
source: Fourth, while place cells across the dorsoventral axis have field sizes that vary over an order of magnitude, spike phase nevertheless usually advances by a maximum of a single theta cycle across their place field indicating that the rate of phase precession varies dorsoventrally (Kjelstrup et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kjelstrup et al., 2008.

claim: CA1 pyramidal cells make few direct connections with one another.
source: CA1 pyramidal cells make few direct connections with one another (Anderson et al., 2007) (but see Yang et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2007, with a caveat citing Yang et al., 2014.

claim: Major sources of input to CA1 include spatially modulated signals from CA3 and from the entorhinal cortex.
source: Major sources of input to CA1 include spatially modulated signals from CA3 and from the entorhinal cortex, and temporally patterned GABAergic inputs from the medial septum, which target hippocampal interneurons and act as a pacemaker to entrain theta oscillations in the circuit (Freund and Antal, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge of CA1 circuitry and a citation to Freund and Antal, 1988.

claim: Temporally patterned GABAergic inputs from the medial septum target hippocampal interneurons and act as a pacemaker to entrain theta oscillations in the circuit.
source: Major sources of input to CA1 include spatially modulated signals from CA3 and from the entorhinal cortex, and temporally patterned GABAergic inputs from the medial septum, which target hippocampal interneurons and act as a pacemaker to entrain theta oscillations in the circuit (Freund and Antal, 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Freund and Antal, 1988.

claim: Many interneurons fire spikes that precess in phase against the theta rhythm.
source: However, many interneurons also fire spikes that precess in phase against the theta rhythm, with interneuron phase precession exhibiting strong functional coupling to individual pyramidal cells (Maurer et al., 2006; Geisler et al., 2007; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maurer et al., 2006; Geisler et al., 2007; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2007.

claim: Interneuron phase precession exhibits strong functional coupling to individual pyramidal cells.
source: However, many interneurons also fire spikes that precess in phase against the theta rhythm, with interneuron phase precession exhibiting strong functional coupling to individual pyramidal cells (Maurer et al., 2006; Geisler et al., 2007; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maurer et al., 2006; Geisler et al., 2007; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2007.

claim: When spontaneously active interneurons integrate spatial signals and theta frequency pacemaker inputs, they generate phase precessing action potentials that can coordinate theta sequences in place cell populations.
source: We show that when spontaneously active interneurons integrate spatial signals and theta frequency pacemaker inputs, they generate phase precessing action potentials that can coordinate theta sequences in place cell populations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model simulations and analyses presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figures 1-3.

claim: The interneuron is driven to fire tonically by a constant depolarizing current.
source: The interneuron is driven to fire tonically by a constant depolarizing current, while pacemaker drive from the medial septum to the interneuron is simulated by an 8 Hz oscillatory current, which is sufficient to fully entrain spiking activity of the interneuron when the pyramidal cell is inactive (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim describes the model setup and is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Pacemaker drive from the medial septum to the interneuron is simulated by an 8 Hz oscillatory current, which is sufficient to fully entrain spiking activity of the interneuron when the pyramidal cell is inactive.
source: The interneuron is driven to fire tonically by a constant depolarizing current, while pacemaker drive from the medial septum to the interneuron is simulated by an 8 Hz oscillatory current, which is sufficient to fully entrain spiking activity of the interneuron when the pyramidal cell is inactive (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model setup and simulation results shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: When spatial input to the pyramidal cell is simulated by a suprathreshold external drive, the resulting synaptic drive to the interneuron initiates phase precession in the coupled pair of cells.
source: When spatial input to the pyramidal cell is simulated by a suprathreshold external drive, the resulting synaptic drive to the interneuron initiates phase precession in the coupled pair of cells, causing their firing frequency to elevate above that of the pacemaker theta and their firing phase to advance continuously over the place field (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: When the pyramidal cell is transiently driven by slow depolarizing current, the phase of spikes fired by the interneuron and by the pyramidal cell advances through a full 360 degrees relative to the 8 Hz pacemaker input.
source: When the pyramidal cell is transiently driven by slow depolarizing current, the phase of spikes fired by the interneuron and by the pyramidal cell advances through a full 360 degrees relative to the 8 Hz pacemaker input.
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results described in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: During injection of a constant input current the model generates either stable phase locking or phase precession at a constant rate against the pacemaker drive depending on the strength of depolarizing drive relative to the strength of pacemaker input.
source: During injection of a constant input current the model generates either stable phase locking or phase precession at a constant rate against the pacemaker drive ('frequency pulling') depending on the strength of depolarizing drive relative to the strength of pacemaker input (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analytical model and simulation results shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: Phase locking occurs for weak drives, where the interneuron becomes entrained to a fixed phase of the pacemaker input.
source: Phase locking occurs for weak drives, where the interneuron becomes entrained to a fixed phase of the pacemaker input.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analytical model and simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Frequency pulling occurs for strong drives, in which case, for a given constant input current, the interneuron oscillates with a fixed frequency difference from the pacemaker, causing its phase to advance continuously relative to the pacemaker input.
source: Frequency pulling occurs for strong drives, in which case, for a given constant input current, the interneuron oscillates with a fixed frequency difference from the pacemaker, causing its phase to advance continuously relative to the pacemaker input.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analytical model and simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the phase locking region, variation in the input current can be used to achieve variation through a maximum of 180 degrees of theta phases.
source: In the phase locking region, because the locking phase varies as a function of the input current, variation in the input current can be used to achieve variation through a maximum of 180 degrees of theta phases (−90 to 90 degrees, see Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analytical model and simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Provided that inputs are sufficiently strong and sustained, the phase of interneuron firing advances through a full 360 degrees, with the rate of phase precession determined by the strength of the injected current.
source: Provided that inputs are sufficiently strong and sustained, the phase of interneuron firing advances through a full 360 degrees, with the rate of phase precession determined by the strength of the injected current (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analytical model and simulation results shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The interneuron remains in a stable phase locking regime while the pyramidal cell is inactive, but enters the frequency pulling regime whenever the pyramidal cell provides sufficient synaptic input, producing phase precession.
source: Specifically, the interneuron remains in a stable phase locking regime while the pyramidal cell is inactive, but enters the frequency pulling regime whenever the pyramidal cell provides sufficient synaptic input, producing phase precession.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model dynamics described in the text and shown in Figures 1-2.

claim: Phase precessing synaptic inputs from the interneuron coordinate the spike timing of the pyramidal cell and confer phase precession.
source: Phase precessing synaptic inputs from the interneuron coordinate the spike timing of the pyramidal cell and confer phase precession, but phase precession in the interneuron is relatively insensitive to the timing of pyramidal cell inputs, instead requiring only a sufficient increase in excitatory drive.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model dynamics described in the text and shown in Figures 1-2.

claim: Phase precession in the interneuron is relatively insensitive to the timing of pyramidal cell inputs, instead requiring only a sufficient increase in excitatory drive.
source: Phase precessing synaptic inputs from the interneuron coordinate the spike timing of the pyramidal cell and confer phase precession, but phase precession in the interneuron is relatively insensitive to the timing of pyramidal cell inputs, instead requiring only a sufficient increase in excitatory drive.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model dynamics described in the text and shown in Figures 1-2.

claim: A linear increase in pacemaker amplitude with running speed, combined with a linear increase in depolarizing current to interneurons with running speed, can generate an approximately linear increase in precession frequency while maintaining stable precession dynamics across running speeds.
source: Indeed, we found that in the minimal circuit model a linear increase in pacemaker amplitude with running speed, combined with a linear increase in depolarizing current to interneurons with running speed, can generate an approximately linear increase in precession frequency while maintaining stable precession dynamics across running speeds (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The predicted dependence on running speed of current input to the interneuron is consistent with findings of a velocity-dependent depolarizing current from glutamatergic circuits in the medial septum to interneurons in CA1.
source: Importantly, the predicted dependence on running speed of current input to the interneuron is consistent with findings of a velocity-dependent depolarizing current from glutamatergic circuits in the medial septum to interneurons in CA1 (Fuhrmann et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fuhrmann et al., 2015.

claim: The predicted dependence of the pacemaker amplitude on running speed is consistent with the dependence on running speed of both the LFP theta amplitude in CA1 and the activity of inhibitory circuitry in the medial septum.
source: Similarly, the predicted dependence of the pacemaker amplitude on running speed is consistent with the dependence on running speed of both the LFP theta amplitude in CA1 (McFarland et al., 1975; Maurer et al., 2005; Patel et al., 2012) and the activity of inhibitory circuitry in the medial septum (King et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McFarland et al., 1975; Maurer et al., 2005; Patel et al., 2012; King et al., 1998.

claim: The phase of theta activity varies systematically across the dorsoventral axis of the hippocampus, spanning a range of 180 degrees.
source: The phase of theta activity varies systematically across the dorsoventral axis of the hippocampus (Lubenov and Siapas, 2009), spanning a range of 180 degrees (Patel et al., 2012) and creating the appearance of a dorsoventral traveling wave.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lubenov and Siapas, 2009 and Patel et al., 2012.

claim: In the reduced interneuron model, the range of phases that stably lock to pacemaker input is precisely 180 degrees, with locking phase depending on the strength of the excitatory current and pacemaker amplitude.
source: In the reduced interneuron model, the range of phases that stably lock to pacemaker input is precisely 180 degrees, with locking phase depending on the strength of the excitatory current and pacemaker amplitude (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the analytical model and simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A gradient in excitatory inputs to interneurons along the dorsoventral axis might be sufficient to generate the observed dorsoventral phase gradient, despite a coherent pacemaker input.
source: This suggests that a gradient in excitatory inputs to interneurons (or alternatively a gradient in input resistance or some intrinsic membrane current) along the dorsoventral axis might be sufficient to generate the observed dorsoventral phase gradient, despite a coherent pacemaker input.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model dynamics described in the text.

claim: The gradient in both phase precession and theta phase along the dorsoventral axis could be accounted for simultaneously by a combination of a dorsoventral gradient in the amplitude of pacemaker drive, the depolarizing current to the interneuron and the strength of excitatory synaptic connections.
source: We found that the gradient in both phase precession and theta phase along the dorsoventral axis could be accounted for simultaneously by a combination of a dorsoventral gradient in the amplitude of pacemaker drive, the depolarizing current to the interneuron and the strength of excitatory synaptic connections (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The model predicts that depolarizing current input to interneurons (or their excitability), the strength of excitatory synaptic connections from pyramidal cells to interneurons and the amplitude of the septal pacemaker drive all decrease from the dorsal pole to the ventral pole of the hippocampus.
source: Thus, our proposed mechanism predicts that depolarizing current input to interneurons (or their excitability), the strength of excitatory synaptic connections from pyramidal cells to interneurons and the amplitude of the septal pacemaker drive all decrease from the dorsal pole to the ventral pole of the hippocampus (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the model results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Theta power is observed to decrease from dorsal to ventral hippocampus.
source: In line with these predictions, theta power is observed to decrease from dorsal to ventral hippocampus (Royer et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Royer et al., 2010.

claim: In open environments, spikes always precess from late to early phases of theta, regardless of running direction.
source: In open environments, spikes always precess from late to early phases of theta, regardless of running direction (Huxter et al., 2008; Climer et al., 2013; Jeewajee et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Huxter et al., 2008; Climer et al., 2013; Jeewajee et al., 2014.

claim: On passes through the edge of the place field, the firing phase advances through around 180 degrees before reversing through 180 degrees over the second half of the field.
source: Experimentally, a more complex feature of phase precession in open environments is observed on passes through the edge of the place field, in which case the firing phase advances through around 180 degrees before reversing through 180 degrees over the second half of the field (Supplementary Figure S2b in Huxter et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Supplementary Figure S2b in Huxter et al., 2008.

claim: In the present model, similar dynamics occur when the interneuron is not driven sufficiently strongly to pass through to the next cycle and is instead attracted back towards the initial phase.
source: In the present model, similar dynamics occur when the interneuron is not driven sufficiently strongly to pass through to the next cycle and is instead attracted back towards the initial phase (Figure 2D–E and Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2D-E and Figure 5A.

claim: The model is consistent with sequences observed during backwards travel, in which theta sequences reflect the ordering at which locations are visited rather than heading direction.
source: Our model is also consistent with sequences observed during backwards travel, in which theta sequences reflect the ordering at which locations are visited rather than heading direction (Cei et al., 2014; Maurer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cei et al., 2014; Maurer et al., 2014.

claim: With strong and sustained inputs to place cells precession continues over multiple theta cycles.
source: We found that with strong and sustained inputs to place cells precession continues over multiple theta cycles (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Over a broad range of input currents, or more directly, a broad range of pyramidal cell spike counts, the interneuron will precess exactly one cycle over the place field.
source: Over a broad range of input currents (Figure 5C), or more directly, a broad range of pyramidal cell spike counts (Figure 5D,E), the interneuron will precess exactly one cycle over the place field.
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Robust phase precession through one cycle in the interneuron occurs provided the place cell fires between 10 and 25 spikes in its place field.
source: For the choice of parameters used here, robust phase precession through one cycle in the interneuron occurs provided the place cell fires between 10 and 25 spikes in its place field.
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results described in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Phase precession resumes upon recovery from transient silencing and pacemaker reset in the model.
source: Indeed, we found that phase precession resumes upon recovery from this perturbation, as observed experimentally (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transient (1 s) silencing of somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons has almost no effect on spike phase, altering mainly the burst firing of place cells.
source: Specifically, transient (1 s) silencing of somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons has almost no effect on spike phase, altering mainly the burst firing of place cells, while silencing of parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons appears to introduce a small shift in average spike phase without compromising phase precession overall (Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Royer et al., 2012.

claim: Silencing of parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons appears to introduce a small shift in average spike phase without compromising phase precession overall.
source: Specifically, transient (1 s) silencing of somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons has almost no effect on spike phase, altering mainly the burst firing of place cells, while silencing of parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons appears to introduce a small shift in average spike phase without compromising phase precession overall (Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Royer et al., 2012.

claim: The model replicates the shift in spike phase of a similar magnitude and direction to that reported in experimental data when interneurons are transiently silenced.
source: When analyzing the resulting data using the methods of Royer and colleagues, we found a shift in spike phase of a similar magnitude and direction to that reported in experimental data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: A single interneuron can support phase precession by more than one place cell, but overlap between the firing fields of place cells coupled to the same interneuron may disrupt precession-based codes.
source: Thus, a single interneuron can support phase precession by more than one place cell, but overlap between the firing fields of place cells coupled to the same interneuron may disrupt precession-based codes by shifting the phase of coding relative to position and by causing multiple cycles of phase precession within a single firing field.
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results described in the text and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The model predicts that outside of their suprathreshold firing fields place cells have subthreshold phase precession fields, characterized by transient increases in the frequency of their theta-modulated inhibitory input when the other place cell is active.
source: As a direct consequence, and in contrast to the case in which there is just one active pyramidal cell per interneuron, the model predicts that outside of their suprathreshold firing fields place cells have subthreshold phase precession fields, characterized by transient increases in the frequency of their theta-modulated inhibitory input when the other place cell is active (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the simulation results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Larger networks successfully compress slow input sequences into fast theta sequences when place field maps are sparse with low overlap.
source: These larger networks successfully compress slow input sequences into fast theta sequences when place field maps are sparse with low overlap (Figure 7A top).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 7A top.

claim: Theta sequences do not emerge when place field maps are dense and have high overlap.
source: In contrast, such sequences do not emerge when place field maps are dense and have high overlap (Figure 7A bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 7A bottom.

claim: Robust single-unit phase precession persists as place field overlap is increased, despite the disruption of single-cycle theta sequences and population phase precession.
source: When we quantified the fidelity of phase precession for individual cells on single laps (see Materials and methods) we found that robust single-unit phase precession persists as place field overlap is increased (Figure 7C, gray line), despite the disruption of single-cycle theta sequences and population phase precession.
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Sequence disruption is caused by a decoherence of phase precession within the population.
source: Thus, sequence disruption is caused by a decoherence of phase precession within the population.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: With increasing amplitude noise injected into pyramidal cells, single-cell phase precession and population sequences were impaired in parallel.
source: We found that with increasing amplitude noise injected into pyramidal cells, single-cell phase precession and population sequences were impaired in parallel (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Increasing noise injected into interneurons disrupts population sequences while leaving phase precession intact at the single trial level.
source: In contrast, increasing noise injected into interneurons disrupts population sequences while leaving phase precession intact at the single trial level, revealing an additional mechanism for dissociating phase precession from population sequences (Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Place field activity is reorganized upon exposure to a novel environment, including a sparsification of the CA1 place code and a decrease in the number of active place cells.
source: Experimental evidence suggests that place field activity is indeed reorganized upon exposure to a novel environment, including a sparsification of the CA1 place code and a decrease in the number of active place cells (Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Frank et al., 2004; Karlsson and Frank, 2008.

claim: Permanent silencing of CA3 would be expected to disrupt CA1 theta sequences without affecting phase precession in the model.
source: Hence, permanent silencing of CA3 would be expected to disrupt CA1 theta sequences without affecting phase precession in our model, as observed by Middleton and McHugh (2016).
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on the model and is consistent with observations by Middleton and McHugh (2016).

claim: Even randomly organized place field maps may be sufficient to account for experimentally observed phase precession statistics in individual place cells.
source: Thus, even randomly organized place field maps may be sufficient to account for experimentally observed phase precession statistics in individual place cells.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4.

claim: Theta sequence compression in conjunction with STDP has been suggested to lead to asymmetry in the firing fields of place cells receiving place cell input.
source: Theta sequence compression in conjunction with STDP has been suggested to lead to asymmetry in the firing fields of place cells receiving place cell input (Mehta et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mehta et al., 2002.

claim: If the downstream US-driven action potential locks to the trough of the theta rhythm, a standard STDP rule will cause inputs from place cells centered on locations before the place where the US was experienced to undergo an increase in synaptic strength.
source: If these downstream action potentials lock to the trough of the theta rhythm, a standard STDP rule will cause inputs from place cells centered on locations before the place where the US was experienced to undergo an increase in synaptic strength (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model and STDP principles, illustrated in Figure 8C.

claim: A downstream neuron which fires at the peak of the theta oscillation will cause a decrease in synaptic strength from neurons representing past locations and an increase in synaptic strength from CA1 pyramidal cells representing the future locations.
source: For example, a downstream neuron which fires at the peak of the theta oscillation will cause a decrease in synaptic strength from neurons representing past locations and an increase in synaptic strength from CA1 pyramidal cells representing the future locations (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model and STDP principles, illustrated in Figure 8D.

claim: Sequence compression with theta oscillations allows locations, or events, occurring in the past or future to be flexibly and selectively associated with a particular outcome by varying the spike phase of the downstream cell.
source: Thus, sequence compression with theta oscillations allows locations, or events, occurring in the past or future to be flexibly and selectively associated with a particular outcome by varying the spike phase of the downstream cell.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model and STDP principles described in the text.

claim: The frequency of theta is established by septal GABAergic projections to hippocampal interneurons.
source: Whereas in many previous models precession is assumed to arise from oscillatory drive targeting place cells, the frequency of theta is established by septal GABAergic projections to hippocampal interneurons (Freund and Antal, 1988), which in turn coordinate the spiking activity of local CA1 pyramidal cells (Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Freund and Antal, 1988 and Royer et al., 2012.

claim: Septal GABAergic projections to hippocampal interneurons coordinate the spiking activity of local CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: Whereas in many previous models precession is assumed to arise from oscillatory drive targeting place cells, the frequency of theta is established by septal GABAergic projections to hippocampal interneurons (Freund and Antal, 1988), which in turn coordinate the spiking activity of local CA1 pyramidal cells (Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Royer et al., 2012.

claim: Only 7–11% of neurons in CA1 are interneurons.
source: While the model that we propose in Figure 1 generates phase precession using only an isolated place cell and interneuron, CA1 place cells are embedded into much larger networks in which only 7–11% of neurons are interneurons (Woodson et al., 1989; Aika et al., 1994; Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Woodson et al., 1989; Aika et al., 1994; Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013.

claim: Intrahippocampal administration of cannabinoids disrupts the temporal organization of CA1 activity during theta cycles without altering firing rates.
source: Intrahippocampal administration of cannabinoids disrupts the temporal organization of CA1 activity during theta cycles without altering firing rates (Robbe and Buzsáki, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Robbe and Buzsáki, 2009.

claim: Reward responsive neurons in the VTA lock more strongly to the hippocampal theta rhythm than non-reward responsive neurons.
source: In line with these predictions, reward responsive neurons in the VTA lock more strongly to the hippocampal theta rhythm than non-reward responsive neurons, and VTA neurons that lock more strongly to the hippocampal theta rhythm exhibit greater coordination with CA1 cell assemblies representing reward locations during awake sharp wave ripple events (Gomperts et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gomperts et al., 2015.

claim: VTA neurons that lock more strongly to the hippocampal theta rhythm exhibit greater coordination with CA1 cell assemblies representing reward locations during awake sharp wave ripple events.
source: In line with these predictions, reward responsive neurons in the VTA lock more strongly to the hippocampal theta rhythm than non-reward responsive neurons, and VTA neurons that lock more strongly to the hippocampal theta rhythm exhibit greater coordination with CA1 cell assemblies representing reward locations during awake sharp wave ripple events (Gomperts et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gomperts et al., 2015.

claim: Reward-encoding neurons in the ventral striatum precess in phase relative to the hippocampal theta rhythm as the animal approaches a reward site.
source: This behavior has been observed in reward-encoding neurons in the ventral striatum, which precess in phase relative to the hippocampal theta rhythm as the animal approaches a reward site (van der Meer and Redish, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to van der Meer and Redish, 2011.

claim: On the first lap of a novel linear track place cells exhibit phase precession, but the phase lags between cells are initially uncoordinated and do not generate population theta sequences until after further experience.
source: For example, on the first lap of a novel linear track place cells exhibit phase precession, in that their spikes advance continuously in phase against the theta rhythm, but the phase lags between cells are initially uncoordinated and do not generate population theta sequences until after further experience (Feng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Feng et al., 2015.

claim: When input from CA3 is permanently absent, robust phase precession is observed in each cell while spatially organized theta sequences fail to emerge.
source: Similarly, when input from CA3 is permanently absent, robust phase precession is observed in each cell while spatially organized theta sequences fail to emerge (Middleton and McHugh, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Middleton and McHugh, 2016.
